'''''Cunninghamia lanceolata''''', [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]] including '''''Cunninghamia sinensis''''', commonly known as '''Chinese fir''', is a [[species]] of tree in the cypress family, [[Cupressaceae]]. It is native to south-central and southeast China.<ref name=POWO_676725-1/> Ornamentally ''C. lanceolata'' is commonly planted as a specimen tree in temperate zones.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web|title=China Fir|url=https://www.uaex.edu/yard-garden/resource-library/plant-week/china-fir-03-27-2015untitled.aspx|access-date=2020-10-13|website=China Fir|language=en|archive-date=2021-09-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210902210204/https://www.uaex.edu/yard-garden/resource-library/plant-week/china-fir-03-27-2015untitled.aspx}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
''[[Cunninghamia konishii]]'' is treated as a distinct species by some sources, although it has also been suggested that it is conspecific with ''C. lanceolata''.<ref name="LuChiaHongHu99" /><ref name="ChunLinTanLin04" /> Though ''C. konishii'' may be treated as the same species, its primary distribution is in Taiwan, where as ''C. lanceolata'' is found in mainland China.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cunninghamia konishii {{!}} Threatened Conifers of the World (en-GB)|url=https://threatenedconifers.rbge.org.uk/conifers/cunninghamia-konishii|access-date=2020-11-17|website=threatenedconifers.rbge.org.uk}}</ref> ''Cunninghamia lanceolata'' was originally described in 1827 by English botanist William J. Hooker.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hooker, William Jackson {{!}} International Plant Names Index|url=https://www.ipni.org/a/4086-1|access-date=2020-11-18|website=www.ipni.org}}</ref>

== Description ==
''Cunninghamia lanceolata,'' commonly known as Chinese fir, is a tall conifer able to reach heights of {{convert|150|ft|m|abbr=off|sp=us}} in mild climates. In North America, the height typically ranges from {{convert|30|to|50|ft|meter|abbr=off|sp=us}}.<ref name=":12"/> In native forest land in China heights can reach up to {{convert|150|ft|m|abbr=off|sp=us}} and {{convert|30|to|70|ft|meter|abbr=off|sp=us}} in a cultivated forest. The crown of the China Fir forms a pyramidal shape. The bark color typically ranges from dark gray to dark browns.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cunninghamia lanceolata (China-fir) description|url=https://www.conifers.org/cu/Cunninghamia_lanceolata.php|access-date=2020-10-27|website=www.conifers.org}}</ref> Foliage consist of spiral leaf arrangements of green lanceolate shaped leaves.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cunninghamia lanceolata - Plant Finder|url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=a159|access-date=2020-11-02|website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref> Male cones form in clusters of 10 to 30 while female cones form in clusters of 2 to 3. Seed cones are small and almost unnoticeable when first pollinated. The cones are mature after 7 months and range in size from {{convert|1|to|1.8|in|cm|abbr=off}} in length.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web|title=Cunninghamia / China fir {{!}} Conifer Genus|url=https://conifersociety.org/conifers/cunninghamia/|access-date=2020-10-13|website=American Conifer Society|language=en}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
''Cunninghamia lanceolata'' is found in central China stretching towards the East Coast of China (including the Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi, Guizhou, Hubei, Hunan, Jiangxi, Sichuan, Yunnan, Zhejiang regions).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cunninghamia lanceolata Chinese Fir PFAF Plant Database|url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Cunninghamia+lanceolata|access-date=2020-11-17|website=pfaf.org}}</ref>

== Ethnobotany ==
In China, ''C. lanceolata'' is sought after for its soft yet highly durable wood and having a scent similar to the coast redwood (''Sequoia sempervirens'') and sugi (''Cryptomeria japonica'').<ref name=":02"/> ''Cunninghamia lanceolata'' has been included in Chinese folklore for over 1000 years and the roots, branches, leaves and bark from the tree have been used for pain relief. Recent studies support the use of various parts of ''C. lanceolata'' to treat pain as well as rheumatic conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Xin|first1=Hai-Liang|last2=Zhai|first2=Xiao-Feng|last3=Zheng|first3=Xu|last4=Zhang|first4=Lei|last5=Wang|first5=Yu-Liang|last6=Wang|first6=Zhuo|date=August 2012|title=Anti-Inflammatory and Analgesic Activity of Total Flavone of Cunninghamia lanceolata|journal=Molecules|language=en|volume=17|issue=8|pages=8842–8850|doi=10.3390/molecules17088842|pmid=22832885|pmc=6268220|doi-access=free}}</ref> ''Cunninghamia lanceolata'' heartwood is also notable for its resistance to termites, rot, and numerous fungi.

== Cultivation ==
In China, roughly 30 percent of all timber plantations are composed of ''C. lanceolata'', which covers an estimated 9 million hectares, primarily in southern China. The China fir is responsible for around 25 percent of all Chinese commercial timber production. Within the past 70 years plantations have tripled in area due to widespread planting and reforestation.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lu|first1=Yuhao|last2=Coops|first2=Nicholas C.|last3=Wang|first3=Tongli|last4=Wang|first4=Guangyu|date=February 2015|title=A Process-Based Approach to Estimate Chinese Fir (Cunninghamia lanceolata) Distribution and Productivity in Southern China under Climate Change|journal=Forests|language=en|volume=6|issue=2|pages=360–379|doi=10.3390/f6020360|doi-access=free|hdl=2429/69631|hdl-access=free}}</ref> ''Cunninghamia lanceolata'' is also used for [[carbon sequestration]]. Under the use of near natural forest management (NNFM), soils have the ability to sequester carbon, and can be utilized to [[climate change mitigation|combat climate change]]. Carbon sequestration from NNFM has been shown to increase carbon stocks in soils with the aid of litter decomposition in topsoil.<ref>{{Cite journal|doi=10.3390/f10080626|doi-access=free|title=The Impact of Near Natural Forest Management on the Carbon Stock and Sequestration Potential of Pinus massoniana (Lamb.) and Cunninghamia lanceolata (Lamb.) Hook. Plantations|year=2019|last1=Ming|first1=Angang|last2=Yang|first2=Yujing|last3=Liu|first3=Shirong|last4=Nong|first4=You|last5=Li|first5=Hua|last6=Tao|first6=Yi|last7=Sun|first7=Dongjing|last8=Lei|first8=Liqun|last9=Zeng|first9=Ji|last10=An|first10=Ning|journal=Forests|volume=10|issue=8|page=626}}</ref>

''Cunninghamia lanceolata'' 'Glauca', blue China fir, is a horticultural variety that is differentiated by it blueish foliage.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cunninghamia lanceolata 'Glauca' {{!}} Landscape Plants {{!}} Oregon State University|url=https://landscapeplants.oregonstate.edu/plants/cunninghamia-lanceolata-glauca|access-date=2020-11-18|website=landscapeplants.oregonstate.edu}}</ref> It grows similarly to China fir with the exception of better winter hardiness.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cunninghamia lanceolata 'Glauca' / blue China fir {{!}} Conifer Trinomial|url=https://conifersociety.org/conifers/cunninghamia-lanceolata-glauca/|access-date=2020-11-18|website=American Conifer Society|language=en}}</ref> There are no known pests or diseases of major concern for ''C. lanceolata''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cunninghamia lanceolata Chinese Fir PFAF Plant Database|url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Cunninghamia+lanceolata|access-date=2020-11-02|website=pfaf.org}}</ref> Brown foliage near the bole is caused from the tree holding onto dead needles for a number of years as the autumn season approaches.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Watson|first=Edward F. Gilman and Dennis G.|date=2014-06-17|title=Cunninghamia lanceolata: China Fir|url=https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/st220|access-date=2020-11-02|website=edis.ifas.ufl.edu|language=en}}</ref> As China fir matures and grows in height as well as width, the crown opens and spaces out and branches become more pendulous despite forming a pyramidal crown at a younger age.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Cunninghamia lanceolata (China Fir) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/cunninghamia-lanceolata/|access-date=2020-11-02|website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref>
